source.title: Unveiling Latent Knowledge in Chemistry Language Models through Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: J. Cohen; Alexander Hasson; Sara Tanovic

record.file_problem: No apparent garbling or truncation; full paper text, including supplementary sections, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Conceptually tests indirect evidence for SAE-recoverable, distributed features in a real chemistry language model by comparing SAE feature measurements with raw-neuron measurements. It does not reproduce the original toy-model method.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results measuring SAE features and raw neurons, including feature detection, descriptor correlations, and ablation. Hyperparameter sweeps used to select a configuration are not included as rows because they do not directly test the listed versions. No cited results from other studies are recorded.
record.test_reason: The study trains TopK SAEs on a 289M chemistry transformer (SMI-TED). It compares SAE features with raw neurons on concept detection, descriptor correlation, toxicity predictors and ablation. This is a new setting with direct results on V4: features are distributed across neurons, and an SAE can recover sparse features. It does not use toy models or test capacity causes, alternative polysemanticity causes, feature canonicality or dimensionality.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that SAEs decompose SMI-TED's latent vectors into a more interpretable, disentangled basis spanning substructures, physicochemical descriptors and functional concepts. They also say these features are causally relevant via ablation, a capability not afforded by the entangled neuron basis. Limitations: single architecture, training-set chemical space, manual interpretation, need for stronger baselines, feature splitting untested.
record.recipe_differences: Applies TopK sparse autoencoders to a chemistry language model's whole-molecule representations and evaluates chemical concepts; it does not use the original toy-network setup or test superposition geometry as a function of feature count and sparsity.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports that reconstruction fidelity varies with SAE sparsity level and expansion factor; the selected main configuration is 8× expansion with k = 80. Its ablation protocols also differ between dense neurons and sparse SAE features.

fits_no_version.finding: The feature-over-neuron advantage is largest for low-prevalence motifs. The authors infer that the model avoids dedicating single neurons to rare concepts, while common motifs have near-dedicated neurons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In real models, frequent features get near-dedicated neurons while rare features are spread across many (a frequency-based analogue of V2, correlational only).

record.peer_reviewed: 39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025) Workshop: AI for Accelerated Materials Design
record.problems: The evidence covers one model architecture. The paper says feature interpretation is not yet scaled, feature generalization outside the training chemical space is open, and stronger baselines are needed. The exact overlap between the SAE training sample and SMI-TED's unreleased training data is unknown. Some ablation outcomes and variability are only shown in figures, and the dense-neuron and SAE-feature ablation protocols differ.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying reported results were left out.

untested.parts: No toy networks, sparsity-dependent transition or feature geometry.
No test of capacity or importance as a cause of polysemanticity; the prevalence pattern is only correlational.
No alternative causes of polysemantic neurons are tested.
Only one chemistry model, one layer (submersion vector), and one SAE configuration (8x, k=80) are analysed. General-domain LLMs are not tested.
Completeness, cross-seed or cross-size stability, uniqueness and canonicality are not tested; feature splitting is only named as future work.
No comparison of 1-D directions against multi-dimensional features.

missing.what: SAE reconstruction fidelity at the selected configuration: FVE ≈0.972 at k=80 (≈0.987 at k=160), plus SMILES reconstruction accuracy across configurations. Needed to judge how much of the representation the dictionary captures.
missing.locator: Section S3.1, Figure S1b, Figure S3a

missing.what: Some SAE features are frequent generalists that activate across structurally diverse molecules and are 'potentially polysemantic' (features 80, 429). This is qualitative only.
A single feature spans three distinct chemotypes sharing opioid-receptor activity, not explained by their maximum common substructure.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed to T3 (new domain, a chemistry LM); the method is not a different approach to the original toy-model question. V5 is dropped as tested: the ablations show causal relevance, not completeness or canonical status, and 'stability' in S5 means valid reconstruction. The neuron and SAE ablation protocols differ (mean vs zero), which weakens the r23 contrast. The study also reports PCA and NMF baselines; PCA is more parsimonious per descriptor but conflates concepts. The paper is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks, feature-versus-dimension sweep, sparsity-dependent geometric transition, or regular feature geometry is tested.
The study does not test whether limited capacity or feature importance causes neurons to become polysemantic, or whether important features obtain dedicated dimensions.
It does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity is evidence of superposition.
Tests one chemistry model and SAE-based recovery in molecular representations; does not test other LLMs or establish how common this representation is across models.
Ablation bears on causal usefulness and some stability of features, but completeness, uniqueness, cross-seed or cross-SAE stability, and canonicality are not established.
Does not compare one-dimensional feature directions against multi-dimensional feature representations.

rows.subject: SMI-TED

rows.baseline: Raw neurons: 69; PCA components: 3; NMF factors: 5
rows.note: The authors state that PCA conflates concepts in fewer dimensions, while these relationships map to 100 distinct SAE features.

rows.subject: SMI-TED

rows.subject: SMI-TED
rows.operation_detail: Compared toxicity prediction using all SAE features versus all raw-neuron activations.
rows.note: The authors describe the performance difference as statistically insignificant and the decomposition as information-preserving for this task.
rows.check: Equal AUCpr (0.606 vs 0.603) is an information-preservation check. It does not measure whether features are distributed or recovered.

rows.subject: SMI-TED
rows.operation_detail: Counted significant toxicity predictors selected by coefficient p-value.
rows.measure: Number and proportion of significant input variables
rows.baseline: Raw neuron basis: 213 neurons (0.277% of variables)
rows.value: SAE feature basis: 19 features (0.003% of variables), with the same reported performance
rows.note: The paper describes the SAE representation as more compact for this prediction task.

rows.subject: SMI-TED
rows.operation_detail: Ablated individual raw neurons by replacing activations with the distribution mean for selected high- and low-activation molecules before decoding.

conditions.value: Each of 768 neurons; 100 molecules with highest and lowest activations per neuron

rows.value: 14 of 768 neurons produced any invalid SMILES; no intervention produced a valid but different molecule
rows.note: The paper interprets this as dense representations being robust and chemical information distributed across many neurons. The intervention differs from the SAE-feature ablation protocol.
rows.check: Individual neuron ablation to the mean changes no molecule, which the authors read as information distributed across many neurons. The protocol (mean ablation) differs from the SAE zero-ablation, so the result is indirect. It does not bear on V5.

rows.subject: SMI-TED
rows.operation_detail: Set each active SAE feature activation to zero before decoding.

conditions.value: 2,501 active features; up to 100 nonzero-activation molecules per feature

rows.measure: Features that steered molecules to new, valid structures
rows.value: 749 of 2,501 active features successfully steered molecules to new, valid chemical structures
rows.note: The paper reports a trade-off between feature stability and steerability; it does not provide text values for the full original/invalid/steered outcome distribution.
rows.check: 749 of 2,501 active features steer to valid new molecules, so a minority of recovered features have this causal effect. The reader's 'stability' means valid reconstruction, not feature stability across SAEs, so the row does not bear on V5.

source_check.correct: state=observed for V4: ablation of 749 recovered SAE features produces new valid structures. The remaining features' steering outcomes do not establish incomplete sparse-feature recovery.
source_check.problem: The partial state imposes universal causal steerability, which V4 does not claim.

rows.subject: SMI-TED
rows.operation_detail: Compared stability of SAE feature steering outcomes using Levenshtein-distance variability.
rows.measure: Standard deviation of Levenshtein distances and its relation to invalid reconstruction rate
rows.value: Text states that more stable and steerable features have low standard deviation; features with higher invalid reconstruction rates also have higher standard deviations. Numerical values are figure-only.
rows.note: The text describes the qualitative relationship, but does not give numeric variability values.
rows.check: Consistency of steering edits (Levenshtein SD) is figure-only and does not measure any version's construct.

relationships.condition: SMI-TED submersion vector, rare and mid-prevalence motifs, descriptors, toxicity, SAE ablation
relationships.reason: SAE features detect rare groups far better than any neuron (r2, r4, r8: e.g. nitrate 1.000 vs 0.056). Descriptors correlate with ~66 neurons vs ~6 features (r15), and toxicity needs 213 neurons vs 19 features (r19). Neuron ablation is inert while SAE ablations edit structure (r20–r23).
relationships.display_finding: SAE features detected rare groups far better than any neuron (nitrate 1.000 vs 0.056). Descriptors correlated with about 66 neurons versus about 6 features, toxicity needed 213 neurons versus 19 features, and neuron ablation was inert while SAE ablations edited structure.

relation.reason: Its own feature-versus-neuron comparisons, descriptor analyses and interventions bear directly on V4.

tranche.reason: The study tests sparse-feature recovery and distributed chemical representations in a new setting: whole-molecule representations of a pretrained chemistry transformer.

source_check.notes: The toxicity percentages are source-level arithmetic inconsistencies; counts and representation sizes are explicitly reported. Neuron ablations replace activations with their mean, whereas SAE ablations set nonzero activations to zero.

statements.correction: SMI-TED maximum F1: alkyl carbon, SAE 0.945 versus neuron 0.938; high-specificity carbonyl, SAE 0.745 versus neuron 0.735. Ablations: 749 of 2,501 active SAE features steer molecules to new valid structures. These results demonstrate recovered features; the steering count measures intervention success.
statements.problem: The SMI-TED facts are accurate, but their classification as limiting V4 is unsupported: V4 requires neither superiority over individual neurons nor successful steering by every active feature.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: SMI-TED on the tested molecular datasets
reader_labels.reason: SAE features detect many functional groups, often outperform raw neurons, and retain comparable toxicity prediction performance with fewer significant predictors (r1–r19); feature ablations also produce targeted or valid molecular changes (r20–r22, r24).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Ablations and steering on the tested SMI-TED/MOSES setup
reader_labels.reason: Some SAE feature ablations steer to valid new molecules, but only 749 of 2,501 active features do so, and the paper reports a stability–steerability trade-off; the results do not establish features as complete or canonical units (r24–r25).
